section.title: Love and the Nearness of the Day
section.sectionRationale: Paul gathers the whole moral life under one continuing debt: love. Having spoken of paying what is owed to the authorities, he turns to the one obligation that is never discharged, to love one another, for love fulfills the law. Then he presses the point with urgency: the night is far gone, the day is at hand, so cast off the works of darkness, put on the armor of light, and clothe yourselves with the Lord Jesus Christ.
section.thesis: The believer owes no one anything except the abiding debt of love, which fulfills the whole law; and because the day of salvation draws near, we must wake from sleep, cast off the works of darkness, and put on the Lord Jesus Christ.
section.frameNote: Two movements: love as the outstanding debt that fulfills the law, summed up in loving your neighbor as yourself; and the nearness of the day, the call to wake, cast off darkness, and put on Christ.

verses.text: Be {{opheilo|indebted}} to no one, except to one another in love. For he who loves his neighbor has fulfilled the {{nomos|law}}.
The commandments “Do not commit adultery,” “Do not murder,” “Do not steal,” “Do not covet,” and any other commandments, are summed up in this one decree: “{{agape|Love}} your neighbor as yourself.”
Love does no wrong to its neighbor. Therefore love is the {{pleroma|fulfillment}} of the law.

units.label: The day is at hand
units.note: put on the Lord Jesus Christ

verses.text: And do this, understanding the occasion. The hour has come for you to wake up from your slumber, for our salvation is nearer now than when we first believed.
The night is nearly over; the day has drawn near. So let us lay aside the deeds of darkness and put on the {{hopla|armor}} of light.
Let us behave decently, as in the daytime, not in carousing and drunkenness, not in sexual immorality and debauchery, not in dissension and jealousy.
Instead, clothe yourselves with the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the desires of the flesh.

opheilo.gloss: To owe, to be indebted, to be under obligation. Paul has just spoken of paying debts to the authorities; now he says to owe no one anything, except the one debt that is never paid off, to love one another. Love is a standing obligation that can never be checked off as complete, for it is always due afresh.

nomos.gloss: Law, especially the law of Moses with its commandments. Paul says the one who loves his neighbor has fulfilled the nomos, for love is what all the commandments were reaching toward. The law is not abolished by love but brought to its intended goal, its every requirement met in the act of genuine love.

agape.gloss: Love, the self-giving love that seeks the good of another. Here it is the sum of the second table of the law: love your neighbor as yourself gathers up the commandments against adultery, murder, theft, and coveting. Agape does no wrong to a neighbor, so wherever it rules, the law is kept.

pleroma.gloss: Fullness, fulfillment, completion. Love is the pleroma of the law: not its cancellation but its filling full, the point at which the law's purpose is realized. Where love reigns, every commandment that guards a neighbor is already satisfied, so love is the law brought to completeness.

hopla.gloss: Weapons or armor, the equipment of a soldier. Paul urges us to put on the hopla of light, the moral armor that befits those who belong to the coming day. It is warfare imagery: the believer strips off the deeds of darkness and takes up the armor of light, ready for the day that is dawning in Christ.

basic.context: Paul has told believers to pay what they owe the authorities. Now he lifts up the one debt that can never be paid off: love. Love, he says, is the fulfillment of the whole law, since every commandment protecting a neighbor is summed up in loving that neighbor as yourself. Then he adds urgency: the night is nearly over and the day is near, so live now as people of the light and clothe yourselves with Christ.
basic.hermeneutics: Read verses 8 to 10 as the summary of all Christian duty in one word, love, and verses 11 to 14 as the motivation, the nearness of the day. The commands are not a ladder to salvation but the fitting life of those already saved and awaiting Christ's return. The passage moves from the debt of love, to the sum of the law, to the urgency of the hour, to the great command to put on Christ Himself.
basic.originalLanguages: Paul plays on opheilo, to owe: owe no one anything except love. The one who loves has fulfilled the nomos, the law, for agape sums up the commandments and does no wrong to a neighbor, so love is the pleroma, the fullness, of the law. And as the day dawns we put on the hopla, the armor, of light.
basic.typology: Love your neighbor as yourself, drawn from Leviticus, reaches its fullness in Christ, who loved to the end and laid down His life. The imagery of night giving way to day echoes the prophets' longing for the dawn of salvation, fulfilled in the first coming of Christ the light and consummated at His return.
basic.christ: The passage climaxes in a Person: put on the Lord Jesus Christ. Christ is Himself the fulfillment of the law and the perfect love it required. He is the light in whom the day dawns, and to clothe ourselves with Him is to be covered in His righteousness and to walk in His likeness. The salvation drawing near is His return in glory.
basic.god: God is the giver of the law that love fulfills and the author of the salvation that draws near. The whole appeal rests on His saving timetable, the day He is bringing to dawn. To live in love and light is to live in step with God's purpose, awake and ready for the day He has appointed in Christ.
basic.crossReferences: Leviticus 19 gives the command to love your neighbor as yourself. Galatians 5 says the whole law is fulfilled in that one command. Ephesians 6 develops the armor of light. Galatians 3 speaks of being clothed with Christ in baptism.
basic.oneStory: The law always aimed at love, and the prophets longed for the dawn of God's salvation. In Christ the true light has come and the day has begun to break. Now His people, clothed with Christ and walking in love, live between the sunrise of His first coming and the full day of His return, when the night of this age will be gone forever.

context.literary:
Verse 8 is a bridge. It looks back to verse 7, where Paul told the church to pay everyone what they owe, and it turns the word 'owe' into a pun: owe nothing to anyone except the debt of loving one another. The shift from taxes to love shows that the apostle sees the whole of public and private duty as a single field. The ordinary obligations of chapter 13 are covered by the one obligation of love, which can never be paid off and so keeps the believer moving toward others.

The passage then turns on the phrase 'and do this' in verse 11. The first half, verses 8 to 10, is about the content of the Christian life, and the second half, verses 11 to 14, about its timing. Love is the what and the nearness of the day is the when. Together they bring the ethical section that began in 12:1 to its close, which is why verse 14 ends on a note that sounds like a summary of the whole: put on the Lord Jesus Christ.

The second half is built on paired images of night and day, sleep and waking, and clothes taken off and put on. The 'deeds of darkness' of verse 12 are named in verse 13 as three pairs: carousing and drunkenness, sexual immorality and debauchery, dissension and jealousy. The first pair concerns appetite for pleasure, the second sexual excess, and the third the sins of the community that tear it apart. The list moves from the private to the social, and ends on strife, which returns the reader to the theme of love.
context.historical:
The imagery of night and day had plain meaning in a city that was loud after dark. Roman writers describe the revels of the night, feasts and drinking parties that ran into the early hours, and the 'beds' in Paul's second pair are the literal term for the bedroom, a place of immorality in the world he knew. A church that lived 'as in the daytime' was recognisably different.

The call to wake from sleep belongs to a longer Jewish and Christian tradition of watchfulness. Jesus told His disciples to keep awake because they did not know the hour, Mark 13:35-37, and Paul told the Thessalonians that they were sons of the day, not of the night, 1 Thessalonians 5:4-8. The early church lived in expectation, and the expectation was a spur to holiness, not an escape from the world.

Paul writes about AD 57, roughly a quarter of a century after the resurrection. His 'nearer now than when we first believed' recognises that time has passed since the believers' conversion and that the end draws closer with each year. The verses became famous in later history: Augustine, in his Confessions, tells how in a garden in Milan he heard a child's voice say 'take and read', opened the book at Romans 13:13-14, and found that the sentence ended his resistance. The passage has been a threshold of conversion for many since.
context.canonical:
The command to love one's neighbour is found in Leviticus 19:18, and Jesus took it as the second of the two great commandments, on which hang all the Law and the Prophets, Matthew 22:37-40. Paul quotes it twice, here and in Galatians 5:14, and James calls it the royal law, James 2:8. The apostle picks the second table of the law, the commands about neighbours, because that is where love is tested. John says the same of love for the brother, 1 John 4:20-21.

The New Testament also expounds this as 'the law of Christ', Galatians 6:2, a phrase that places the commandments inside the pattern of Jesus' self-giving. Love does not abolish the commandments; Paul cites them. It supplies their motive and reach.

The second half draws from the prophetic expectation of the day of the Lord. The prophets spoke of a day of darkness for the wicked and light for the righteous, Amos 5:18-20 and Malachi 4:2. The New Testament's 'day' is the day of Christ's return, 1 Thessalonians 5:2-8 and 2 Peter 3:10. The language of clothing returns throughout Scripture: Isaiah 59:17 pictures the Lord putting on righteousness as a breastplate, Zechariah 3:1-5 describes the high priest's filthy clothes exchanged for splendid robes, and Ephesians 6:11-17 and Colossians 3:12 draw the lines directly into the Christian's armour and garments. Romans 13:14 is the summary of this whole tradition in one sentence.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul wanted the Roman believers to see that the shape of the Christian life is simpler than the sum of its rules. He is not abolishing the commandments. He is saying that someone who keeps loving will end up keeping all of them, because each of them is a specific form of not harming a neighbour. This was particularly important in a church divided over food and holy days, as chapters 14 and 15 show. Love is the thing that stops one group treating the other's practices as a battleground.

He also wanted the church to feel the urgency of its situation. People can live as though the present order is permanent, and the apostle breaks that illusion. The 'hour' has come to wake up. The point is not to calculate dates but to live with the awareness that the Lord is coming, and that makes the moral choices of today matter.

Finally he wanted them to understand that holiness is not a project of self-improvement. The last command is not 'try harder' but 'put on' a person. The believer is to take Christ as a garment and then not give any room, 'provision', for the flesh. The apostle's remedy for sin is the positive presence of Christ, not only the avoidance of the negative.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
These verses are written as commands and are for everyone. Owe love; do not let any debt of love go unpaid; wake up; lay aside darkness; put on the armour of light; clothe yourselves with Christ. The passage speaks as an exhortation to people who are already saved, not as instructions for earning salvation.

A few cautions help in applying them. The warning 'be indebted to no one' is not a ban on borrowing; the context is paying what is owed without delay, and elsewhere Scripture permits lending and borrowing, though it counsels care, Proverbs 22:7. The nearness of the day is a motive, not a timetable. Past generations of Christians have been wrong when they predicted the date, and Paul himself says only that salvation is closer than it was. And the statement that love fulfils the law is not a claim that love can be defined without the commandments. The listing of adultery, murder, theft and covetousness shows that love has content. Where the commandments say what harms a neighbour, love will not do it.

debates.question: What does Paul mean that our salvation is nearer than when we first believed?

views.label: The nearness of Christ's return and final salvation
views.case: The historic reading takes salvation as the completed salvation at Christ's return, the redemption of the body; each passing day brings that consummation nearer, so believers live in wakeful readiness.

views.label: A general sense of spiritual urgency
views.case: Some soften it to a call for moral seriousness without a specific reference to the second coming; but the imagery of night and day points to the approaching day of the Lord.

debates.bearing: Either way the passage summons wakeful, holy living; the historic reading grounds that urgency in the certain return of Christ, when salvation will be brought to completion.

debates.question: How does love fulfill the law without abolishing it?

views.label: Love brings the law to its intended goal
views.case: The historic reading holds that love does not set the commandments aside but accomplishes their aim; since love does no wrong to a neighbor, the one who loves has already kept every commandment that guards him.

views.label: Love replaces the law entirely
views.case: Some read Paul as discarding the law for a vague ethic of love; but Paul cites the specific commandments and says love fulfills, that is fills full, rather than cancels them.

debates.bearing: The orthodox reading keeps law and love together: love is the fulfillment of the law, its every neighbor-protecting command satisfied wherever genuine love reigns.

debates.question: Does 'put on the Lord Jesus Christ' refer to baptism, to obedience, or to union with Christ?

views.label: A command to live out the new identity
views.case: Paul says elsewhere to put on the new self, Ephesians 4:24, and to put on compassion and kindness, Colossians 3:12. On this reading verse 14 is a call to live as someone who already belongs to Christ, which is the fruit of the faith already received.

views.label: A recollection of baptism
views.case: Galatians 3:27 says that those baptised into Christ have clothed themselves with Christ, so some think Paul is recalling the clothing associated with baptism. The command would then mean to live out what was sealed there.

views.label: A call to bring Christ's character to every situation
views.case: Others stress the personal object: not 'put on virtues' but 'put on the Lord Jesus Christ', so that the believer meets each decision asking what Christ would do and in whose strength.

debates.bearing: The readings fit together. Union with Christ was given, symbolised in baptism, and is to be lived in daily conduct. The weight of the verse falls on the Person rather than on a program.

study.originalLanguages:
The verb of verse 8, opheilo, 'to owe', is repeated in a pun: 'owe no one anything', mēdeni mēden opheilete, a double negative for emphasis, 'except to love one another'. The debt is of an unusual kind because paying it increases it. In verse 8 the object of love is ton heteron, literally 'the other', anyone who is not oneself, before verses 9 and 10 use the more familiar plesion, 'neighbour'. The first phrase widens the field of love beyond the fellow believer.

The perfect tense of 'has fulfilled', peplerōken, says that the one who loves stands in the state of having completed the law. 'Fulfilled' is the verb for filling a vessel to the brim, and the noun in verse 10, pleroma, 'fullness', is its partner: love is not a replacement for the law but its full measure. The word 'summed up' in verse 9, anakephalaioo, is the same one used of God's plan to unite all things in Christ in Ephesians 1:10, and it means to bring under a single head. The commandments are headed up by one.

The commandments Paul lists come from the second half of the Ten, and in an order, adultery, murder, theft, which also appears in Luke 18:20 and differs from the Hebrew text of Exodus 20. The word for 'covet' is epithymeo, the verb of desire that returns in verse 14 as the noun 'desires', epithymiai. The temptation Paul names at the end of the passage is the one the tenth commandment named at the start.

Verse 11 speaks of the kairos, 'occasion' or 'season', not the ordinary word for time, chronos, and of the hora, 'hour'. 'Wake up' is egertheinai, the passive of egeiro, which is also the word for being raised from the dead. 'Has drawn near', engiken, is a perfect tense: it has arrived at the near position and stays there. The 'night' has 'advanced', prokopto, a verb used for progress along a road.

The pair of verbs, 'lay aside' (apotithemi) and 'put on' (enduo), is the clothing language of the passage. 'Armour' translates hopla, a general word for weapons or equipment, and the same word appears in Romans 6:13, where believers are told not to present their members as 'instruments' of wickedness but as instruments of righteousness. The 'behave decently' of verse 13 is euschemonos, 'in a seemly way', literally with good shape, the opposite of the 'conforming' in 12:2.

The final phrase, 'make no provision', is pronoia, forethought. The prohibition is not on having desires but on planning for their gratification.

typology.type: The second table of the law and the neighbour, Leviticus 19
typology.fulfillment: Leviticus 19 arranges commands about harvest, wages, justice, speech and the care of foreigners around the refrain 'I am the LORD', and culminates in loving the neighbour as oneself, verse 18. In Christ the whole chapter finds a person to match it. He is the neighbour who stops for the wounded stranger in His own parable, Luke 10:25-37, and He lays down His life for His friends, John 15:13. Paul's claim that love fulfils the law is therefore christological: the law's aim is embodied. The type falls short because the law could name the neighbour but could not supply the heart that loves him, a gift of the Spirit, Romans 5:5.

typology.type: The coming day of the LORD, Amos 5 and Malachi 4
typology.fulfillment: Amos warned that the day of the LORD would be darkness and not light for those who presumed on it, Amos 5:18-20, and Malachi promised the sun of righteousness rising with healing in its wings, Malachi 4:2. In Christ the dawn has begun: the true Light has come into the world, John 1:9, and the night is passing, 1 John 2:8. The correspondence will be completed at His appearing, when He judges the living and the dead. The type shows that the day is both promise and threat, and that waking and watchfulness are therefore the right posture.

Joshua the high priest stands before the angel in filthy clothes, and is told his iniquity has been removed and that he will be clothed with splendid robes. It is a picture of grace that precedes conduct: the garment is given first. Paul's 'put on the Lord Jesus Christ' has the same shape, because the believer receives Christ as righteousness, 1 Corinthians 1:30, and then lives in what has been given. The correspondence is deepened in Christ, who is Himself the High Priest and the clothing. The type falls short in that Joshua was clothed for one office and a limited time, while believers are clothed with the Son.

typology.type: The warrior's armour of the LORD, Isaiah 59:17
typology.fulfillment: In Isaiah, the LORD puts on righteousness as a breastplate and a helmet of salvation, to put right a world with no one to intercede. Paul takes this armour and gives it to the church: 'the armor of light' here, the breastplate of faith and love and the helmet of the hope of salvation in 1 Thessalonians 5:8, the full armour of God in Ephesians 6:13-17. The Lord's own dress becomes the believer's, because the people are in union with the Warrior. The type is fulfilled in Christ, who wins the victory, and the church fights only by standing in His.

study.christ:
The command at the end of the passage is not to a program but to a person: 'clothe yourselves with the Lord Jesus Christ'. Everything that precedes it hangs on Him. He is the one who answered the law's demand perfectly: Matthew 5:17 says He came not to abolish the Law but to fulfil it, and Romans 10:4 calls Him its goal. The believer who loves is therefore not doing something extra to Christ's work but sharing in the life of the One who completed it. Love 'fulfils the law' for us because He first did.

The love that Paul commands has a shape, and its shape is the cross. 'Love one another as I have loved you', John 13:34, and the standard is 'greater love has no one than this', John 15:13. In Galatians 6:2 Paul calls this 'the law of Christ'. When we ask what it means to do no wrong to a neighbour, the answer is in Philippians 2:3-8 and Ephesians 5:2.

The day that is near is the day of His return. The New Testament calls it 'the day of Christ' and 'the appearing of our great God and Savior, Jesus Christ', Titus 2:13. Christ is the light of the world, John 8:12, the 'morning star', Revelation 22:16, and the 'sun of righteousness' of Malachi 4:2 in the reading the church has long given. The night is passing because the Light has risen; the day will be full because He will come.

To 'put on' Christ draws on the language of union. Galatians 3:27 says that in baptism believers have clothed themselves with Christ, and Colossians 3:10-12 describes the new self as renewed in His image. This is not a costume that hides what lies beneath: it is the exchange of Zechariah 3, in which the guilty person is given a righteousness not his own, 2 Corinthians 5:21, and is then expected to walk in it.

A caution is needed. It is not necessary to claim that every detail of the night and day images points to a specific event in Jesus' life. The links above rest on the New Testament's own words about love, light and clothing, and on the fact that the passage places Christ at the centre of the final command.
study.god:
The passage shows God as the giver of a law whose heart is love. The commandments are not a set of arbitrary taboos but a description of what it means not to wrong a neighbour. That implies something about God's character. When He says do not murder, steal or covet, He is telling us how those made in His image should treat each other. The law is His love expressed as a boundary, and Jesus summarised the whole as love for God and for neighbour.

God is also the author of a timetable. The 'occasion' of verse 11 and the 'day' of verse 12 are His. History is moving toward an appointed end, which He will bring in His own time, Acts 17:31. He is not a distant watchmaker, and the sense that the day is nearer is rooted in His promise. Peter adds that the Lord's apparent delay is patience, wanting all to come to repentance, 2 Peter 3:9, which keeps nearness and patience together.

The passage shows God as the Father who clothes His people. The command to put on Christ assumes that He has made a garment available. The God who clothed Adam and Eve, Genesis 3:21, who dressed Joshua in new robes, Zechariah 3:4, and who wrapped His servant in a robe of righteousness, Isaiah 61:10, is the God who gives His Son to be worn. He does not merely forbid the old life; He supplies the new one.

There is a quiet tension in the text. The salvation 'nearer now than when we first believed' implies that the believers were already saved. Paul speaks in Romans of salvation in the past, we were saved in hope, 8:24, in the present, being saved, and in the future, shall be saved, 5:9-10. God's salvation has a beginning and an end, and the passage lives between the two. The believer is secure, and the believer is still urged to wake.

In worship, the text calls the church to hold together delight in God's law and longing for His day. A congregation that has learned to love as God commands, and to watch as God summons, will pray 'Come, Lord Jesus' and mean it, Revelation 22:20, and will find that the same God who gave the law and the day is giving the strength to keep them.

crossReferences.note: The source of the command Paul calls the summary of the commandments. Set in a chapter that repeats 'I am the LORD', it shows that love for the neighbour was always grounded in the character of God, not left to human sentiment, and that it reaches the foreigner as well, Leviticus 19:34.

Jesus names love for God and love for neighbour as the two commandments on which all the Law and the Prophets depend. Paul's summary of the second table in one word is the apostolic echo of this teaching, and it keeps love for neighbour tied to love for God.

The entire law is fulfilled in a single decree, love your neighbour, and Paul warns against using freedom as an opportunity for the flesh, which is the sense in which Romans 13:14 forbids provision for the flesh. Freedom and love are partners.

James calls the same command the royal law and warns that partiality breaks it. It shows how far the command reaches, into the way a church seats its rich and poor, and confirms that 'summing up' does not mean reducing.

The nearest parallel to the night and day imagery: believers are sons of the day, so they are to be awake and sober and to put on the breastplate of faith and love. It supplies a fuller version of the armour of light and shows that watchfulness and love belong together.

The full armour of God is built of truth, righteousness, readiness, faith, salvation and the Word. It expands the 'armor of light' of Romans 13:12 and makes it clear that the armour is received from God, not made by the believer.

For all of you who were baptised into Christ have clothed yourselves with Christ. It supplies the foundation for Romans 13:14: the garment has been given, and the command is to live in what has been received.

Put to death what is earthly, put off anger and slander, put on compassion, kindness, humility and, above all, love, which binds everything together. It shows the same pattern of taking off and putting on, and ends where Romans 13 begins, with love as the bond.

Creation groans and believers wait for the redemption of the body, saved in hope. It explains the sense in which salvation is still to come, and why Paul can say it is nearer now than when they first believed.

The grace of God teaches believers to renounce ungodliness and to live self-controlled, upright and godly lives while waiting for the blessed hope, the appearing of our great God and Saviour Christ Jesus. It is the same logic as Romans 13:11-14, in which the coming day shapes today's conduct.

study.oneStory:
The story begins with a world made in love. God spoke, and the creatures He made were to love Him and each other, but the fall turned human desire inward. Cain's question, 'Am I my brother's keeper?' Genesis 4:9, is the voice of a humanity that treats the neighbour as a threat. The history that follows is the history of owed debts unpaid: of violence, theft and lust, the very things Paul lists.

The law of Sinai set boundaries around that disorder, and its heart was already love, Deuteronomy 6:5 and Leviticus 19:18. But the law could instruct and condemn; it could not change the heart. The prophets promised a day when God would give a new heart and put His Spirit within His people, Ezekiel 36:26-27, and a day of the LORD in which the wicked would be judged and the righteous would see the sun rise with healing.

Romans 13 stands in the interval between the first dawn and the full day. The Son has come, the Spirit has been given, and the love that the law demanded is now being formed in people. The night is not yet over, so believers are still tempted by carousing and strife. But they are called to live now as those who belong to the day that is coming.

The end of the story is what this passage looks toward. In the new creation there is no night, 'for the Lord God will give them light', Revelation 22:5, and the debt of love will be a joy and not a labour. The nations will walk in the city's light, Revelation 21:24, and the tree of life will be for their healing, Revelation 22:2. The clothing of Christ that believers take up now will be seen in its fullness when the Bride is dressed in fine linen, Revelation 19:7-8. What began in a garden where love was unspoiled ends in a city where it can never be spoiled again, and Romans 13 is a letter from the road between.

quiz.q: What is the one debt Paul says we always owe?

options.text: To love one another, a debt that is never fully paid off.
options.note: Owe no one anything except to love one another.

options.text: To repay every financial obligation and nothing more.
options.note: Paul moves beyond money to the standing debt of love.

options.text: To keep the ceremonial law perfectly.
options.note: Paul sums up duty in love, which fulfills the law's aim.

options.text: Nothing; believers owe no obligation of any kind.
options.note: Paul names love as the one continuing obligation.

quiz.q: How does love relate to the law, according to Paul?

options.text: Love fulfills the law, for it does no wrong to a neighbor.
options.note: Love is the fullness of the law, satisfying its every neighbor-protecting command.

options.text: Love abolishes and replaces the law entirely.
options.note: Paul says love fulfills, fills full, rather than cancels the law.

options.text: Love and the law have nothing to do with each other.
options.note: Paul ties them tightly: love is the fulfillment of the law.

options.text: Love makes the commandments harder to keep.
options.note: Love is the very thing the commandments aimed at, not an added burden.

quiz.q: Why does Paul call believers to wake from sleep in verse 11?

options.text: Because salvation is nearer now than when we first believed.
options.note: The nearness of the day is the ground of the urgent call to wake.

options.text: Because they had literally overslept.
options.note: Sleep is a picture of moral drowsiness, not literal sleep.

options.text: Merely to be generally more productive.
options.note: The urgency is rooted in the approaching day of salvation, not mere productivity.

options.text: Because the day of grace has already ended.
options.note: The day is dawning, not ended; salvation draws near.

quiz.q: What is the climactic command of the passage in verse 14?

options.text: Clothe yourselves with the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh.
options.note: The passage rises to putting on Christ Himself.

options.text: Withdraw entirely from the world and its people.
options.note: Paul calls for putting on Christ and walking in love, not withdrawal.

options.text: Indulge the desires of the flesh in moderation.
options.note: Paul says to make no provision for the desires of the flesh.

options.text: Keep the ceremonial law more strictly.
options.note: The climax is putting on Christ, not stricter ceremony.

quiz.q: What does Paul mean by the armor of light in verse 12?

options.text: The moral equipment of those who belong to the coming day, put on in place of the deeds of darkness.
options.note: Believers strip off darkness and take up the armor of light for the dawning day.

options.text: Literal weapons for physical battle against rulers.
options.note: The armor is moral and spiritual, not literal weaponry.

options.text: A guarantee of ease and comfort in this life.
options.note: It is armor for holy living and readiness, not a promise of comfort.

options.text: A private feeling with no effect on conduct.
options.note: The armor of light shows itself in decent, daytime conduct.

questions: Paul calls love the one debt we never finish paying. Who has God placed near you as a neighbor to love, and how is that debt still outstanding?
Love fulfills the law because it does no wrong to a neighbor. Where would genuine love reshape the way you treat someone this week?
Paul says salvation is nearer than when we first believed. How would living in light of Christ's certain return change your priorities today?
The passage calls you to cast off the works of darkness. Is there a deed of darkness God is asking you to lay aside as one who belongs to the day?
To put on the Lord Jesus Christ is the great command here. What would it look like, practically, to clothe yourself with Christ and make no provision for the flesh tomorrow morning?

translationNotes.note: Be indebted to no one plays on the word opheilo, to owe, echoing the debts of verse 7; the one exception is the continuing debt of love, which is never discharged but always freshly due.
Love is the fulfillment of the law renders pleroma, fullness or completion; love does not abolish the commandments but brings them to their intended goal, since love does no wrong to a neighbor.

Clothe yourselves with, or put on, the Lord Jesus Christ uses clothing imagery echoed in Galatians 3:27; the footnote notes the verb can be rendered put on, as in verse 12. These verses were famously instrumental in the conversion of Augustine.
